PAPER
Special Section on Forefront Computing
Loop Unrolling and DFG Partitioning for CGRAs: A Case Study of
The Lattice Boltzmann Method
Toshiyuki ICHIBA†a), Member, Yasuhiro WATANABE†, Nonmember, and Takahide YOSHIKAWA†, Member
SUMMARY
Driven by the strong demand for enhanced performance in High-
Performance Computing (HPC), Coarse-Grained Reconﬁgurable Architec-
tures (CGRAs) are promising technologies that oﬀer high performance even
under power consumption constraints. Performance on CGRAs is signiﬁ-
cantly inﬂuenced by loop unrolling, a technique that increases computational
parallelism by utilizing more processing elements in CGRAs. Determining
the optimal loop unrolling factor is challenging in applications with multiple
loops. This paper presents a case study demonstrating the determination
of optimal loop unrolling factors for an application based on the Lattice
Boltzmann Method (LBM). Because the application’s process exceeds the
capacity of a single CGRA, this paper proposes a method for partitioning
the process to ﬁt the CGRA’s resources using integer linear programming
(ILP). Finally, this paper provides a performance estimation of the CGRAs
runtime and demonstrates the eﬀectiveness of CGRAs for HPC.
key words:
CGRA, HPC, Lattice Boltzmann method, DFG partitioning,
integer linear programming
1.
Introduction
Power-eﬃcient accelerators are widely used in High Perfor-
mance Computing (HPC). While Graphic Processor Units
(GPUs) dominate the current market, research continues on
alternative architectures such as Field-Programmable Gate
Arrays (FPGAs) and Coarse-Grained Reconﬁgurable Archi-
tectures (CGRAs) [1, 2]. CGRAs are reported to provide
higher performance per power consumption compared to
GPUs and FPGAs [3, 4].
Reasons for this include that
CGRAs are dataﬂow architectures conﬁgurable to the ap-
plication, unlike GPUs, and they have a coarser granularity
compared to FPGAs [3]. While GPUs repeatedly perform
steps of reading data, performing operations, and writing
back the results, CGRAs can reconﬁgure the ﬂow of data
and operations tailored to the application as a hardware. In
terms of reconﬁgurability, CGRAs and FPGAs are similar,
but CGRAs’ coarser reconﬁguration granularity gives it su-
perior power performance compared to FPGAs. In some
cases, CGRAs’ power eﬃciency are more than 10 times bet-
ter than that of GPUs [4].
One of the major workloads in HPC is Computational
Fluid Dynamics (CFD) simulation. Examples include sim-
ulations of blood and cancer cell separation [5], droplet and
aerosol dispersion [6], and bubbles collapsing in a ﬂuid that
can damage machinery [7]. These have been nominated for
the Gordon Bell Prize, a prominent award in HPC. One of the

implementations of CFD simulations, the Lattice Boltzmann
Method (LBM) based on the D2Q37 model, is available as
open source software [8] and is part of the SPEChpc 2021
benchmark [9].
Although many studies have implemented programs on
CGRAs, there is limited research on optimizing HPC ap-
plications for CGRAs. In particular, an optimization called
loop unrolling has a signiﬁcant impact on execution perfor-
mance in CGRAs. However, because loop unrolling is a
trade-oﬀbetween CGRA resource consumption and perfor-
mance improvement, determining the optimal factor of loop
unrolling is challenging for processes with multiple loops.
This paper presents a case study of loop unrolling targeting
D2Q37 LBM containing multiple loops and also proposes
a partitioning method to accommodate the use of multiple
CGRAs.
Finally, performance estimates are presented to
indicate the eﬀectiveness of CGRAs in HPC.
This paper is organized as follows: Section 2 provides
an overview of CGRAs, the assumed architecture, and the
compilation ﬂow for CGRAs.
Section 3 details the pro-
cessing structure of the target LBM. Section 4 describes the
optimization details. Related work is discussed in Sect. 5,
and conclusions are presented in Sect. 6.
2.
Coarse-Grained Reconﬁgurable Architectures
2.1
Classiﬁcation of CGRAs
CGRAs are a generic term for various architectures featur-
ing many Processing Elements (PEs) whose computational
content and interconnections are reconﬁgurable. This pa-
per classiﬁes CGRAs from two perspectives: context and
computing model.
First, CGRAs can be classiﬁed as single-context or
multi-context (time-multiplexing). Single-context CGRAs
maintain a single conﬁguration throughout execution,
while multi-context CGRAs support multiple conﬁgurations,
switched periodically. Although multi-context CGRAs can
utilize more PEs than physically available, enabling larger
applications on smaller CGRAs, this comes at the cost of
reduced throughput due to the inability to obtain output ev-
ery cycle [10].
Multi-context CGRAs are often deemed
less power eﬃcient than single-context CGRAs due to the
extra circuitry needed for conﬁguration switching, which
consumes additional power [11]. Furthermore, a report in-
dicates a 36% increase in the area needed to support multi-
context [12].

Second, CGRAs can be classiﬁed based on their com-
puting model as either statically-scheduled or elastic.
In
statically-scheduled CGRAs, the timing of loads/stores and
operations is determined at compile time. In contrast, elastic
CGRAs compute in the data-ﬂow paradigm, operating when
data arrives. Although this eliminates compile-time schedul-
ing and simpliﬁes compiler design, it necessitates additional
circuits for inter-PE data transfer. Therefore, it is reported
that the area and power consumption will increase by more
than 40% [13].
Both multi-context and elastic approaches have their
own advantages and disadvantages. While both features are
expected to improve the ease of application development for
CGRAs, they also increase area and/or power consumption,
creating a trade-oﬀ.
2.2
Assumed CGRA
This paper focuses on HPC applications. In HPC, high exe-
cution performance is often prioritized over ease of applica-
tion development.
Furthermore, to facilitate easier hard-
ware implementation, this paper assumes single-context,
statically-scheduled CGRAs with a simpliﬁed architecture:
PE operations execute in ﬁxed cycles, and data ﬂow between
PEs is unidirectional. The number of PEs in the CGRA is

assumed to be greater than that in the existing CGRAs to
support large HPC applications.
Figure 1 shows an assumed CGRA structure.
The
CGRA has 32 × 32 PEs in a 2D array. PEs can perform
single-precision ﬂoating-point (FP32) operations. The top
row of PEs can load two FP32 data from the local memory,
and the bottom row of PEs can store one FP32 data in the lo-
cal memory. This structure was adopted to reduce memory
read/write operations due to data input/output limitations and
to achieve high throughput by allowing multiple PEs to per-
form pipeline processing. This is similar to the mechanism
used in systolic array accelerators such as Google TPU [14].
Data between PEs ﬂows from up to down, including
diagonally; PEs can perform an operation on the input data
or output the data without any operation. A single PE has
the conﬁguration shown in Fig. 2. Each PE receives a total
of ﬁve input lines: three from above, one from the PE to its
top-left, and one from the PE to its top-right. The output is
also ﬁve lines, but since the data is output in the same way
in three directions, there are only three unique output values.
PE has a Function Unit capable of addition, subtraction, mul-
tiplication, fused multiply-add, and reciprocal operations† in
FP32. The operations are denoted fadd, fsub, fmul, fma,
and frecpe, respectively. All operations are assumed to be
performed in 1 cycle at 1 GHz. Therefore, it takes 32 cycles
to move data from the top row to the bottom row of CGRA.
Each PE contains a register for storing constant values, which
are shown as imm0 and imm1 in Fig. 2. This register is set
during conﬁguration, which sets the operation contents and
connections of each PE, and the register’s values cannot be
changed during runtime. Furthermore, because the register
is located within the PE, it is not included in the count of ﬁve
input data for the PE.
2.3
Compilation Flow for CGRAs
There are three steps to the compiling ﬂow of a program for
CGRAs: the generation of the Data Flow Graph (DFG), the
optimization process of the DFG to CGRAs, and the map-

ping process that determines the correspondence between the
DFG and CGRA. Nodes in the DFG represent the operations,
and edges represent the connections between the operations.
The mapping process uses the DFG as input to determine
the operations and connections of each PE in CGRA. After
mapping, the DFG can be executed in CGRA. For example,
if a DFG with six operations is generated such as Fig. 3, it
can be mapped as shown in Fig. 4. Since input data can only
be loaded from the top row of PEs, input data to node 𝑣3 is
passed through the PE to which node 𝑣2 is assigned in Fig. 4.
In order to achieve high performance, it is important
for the mapping to use as many PEs of CGRA as possi-
ble. Because the mapping problem is an NP-complete prob-
lem [15], various algorithms and tools have been proposed
for the mapping process [11,16–21]. Typical optimization of
the DFG, which is the input to the mapping process, is loop
unrolling. Additionally, DFG partitioning, which partitions
the DFG to ﬁt the size of CGRAs, is also important when
running HPC applications on CGRAs. This paper focuses on
loop unrolling and DFG partitioning rather than on mapping.
Generating DFGs from programs is readily achievable with
existing compiler technology, so the details are not described
here.
3.
Lattice Boltzmann Method
3.1
Overview
LBM is a computational method for ﬂuid simulation, in
which the ﬂuid is approximated by a large number of particles
in a lattice, and the steps of computation of collision and
propagation (or streaming) of the particles are repeated. The
actual equations depend on a model, which is determined by
the dimension of the lattice and the number of particles used
in the computation. In this paper, we focus on the complex
D2Q37 model, which can correctly reproduce the equation
of state of the ﬂuid, regarded as a perfect gas [22]. The
D2Q37 model has substantially more severe requirements
than earlier models, such as a D2Q9 and a D3Q13, both
for the ﬂoating-point units and the memory interface of the
processor [22]. There are optimizations to the GPUs [8,22],
but none to CGRAs. In LBM, the collision kernel is known
to be dominant with respect to the simulation runtime. In
the implementation code of the D2Q37 model [8] targeted
in this paper, the propagation is a data copy, and there is no
computational process. Therefore, this paper considers the
execution of the collision kernel on the CGRAs.
Figure 5 shows the outline structure of the collision ker-
nel.
The loop consists of a triple nested loop with ﬁve
innermost loops. Due to the D2Q37 model, the innermost
loop iterates a ﬁxed 37 times. Because processing exists
between the ﬁve innermost loops, it is called an imperfectly
nested loop. If the nested loop has only the innermost loop,
it is called a perfectly nested loop. The ix and iy loops can
be executed in parallel due to the absence of data dependen-
cies. Therefore, the ﬁve innermost loops and the processing
between them are collectively the targets of execution on the

3.2
Details of Target Collision Kernel

each processing unit in the collision kernel. Scalar variables,
array constants, and array variables are counted separately
in loads/stores because the diﬀerence appears when loop

constants loads presents a problem, as it easily exceeds the

4.
DFG Optimization
Section 4.1 outlines three key considerations for optimizing
a DFG for CGRAs. Sections 4.2 through 4.4 detail the spe-
ciﬁc optimizations applied to the DFG generated from LBM
for each of these considerations. Section 4.5 describes the
automation of DFG partitioning. Section 4.6 estimates the
performance of the LBM.
4.1
Optimization Flow
The following optimization steps are required to execute a
DFG generated from source code on CGRAs.
1. Adapting kernel processing and control structures to the
target CGRAs
2. Applying loop unrolling
3. DFG partitioning
First, it is necessary to conﬁrm whether the operations
and data types of the processing to be executed are supported
by the target CGRAs. For example, CGRAs that only sup-
ports integer types cannot execute ﬂoating-point operations.
Additionally, if the processing includes mathematical func-
tions such as sqrt, sin, or cos, and because many CGRAs
do not support these, it is necessary to replace them with
approximate formulas or similar methods.
Furthermore,
control structures such as if statements and loop statements
should also be converted to structures supported by the target
CGRA.
In CGRAs, higher performance can be achieved by ap-
plying loop unrolling as much as the resources allow in the
form of spatial mapping and increasing the number of paral-
lel computations. If reduction operations are included, it is
important to apply an optimization called tree height reduc-
tion in addition to loop unrolling [23]. Tree height reduction
increases execution performance because the operations are
executed in parallel. To apply loop unrolling, it’s necessary
to determine the unrolling factor while considering the target
CGRAs constraints such as the number of data inputs/outputs
and the number of operations.
When executing a DFG larger than a single CGRA’s
capacity, it is necessary to consider DFG partitioning and
execution across multiple CGRAs. When partitioning, it is
desirable to minimize both the number of CGRAs required
and the amount of data transfer between CGRAs. Further-
more, to execute the partitioned DFGs on CGRAs, CGRA
constraints must be satisﬁed, so a partitioning method that
takes this into account is required. The DFG that can be
executed in the target CGRA has depth constraints.
The
depth of the DFG is deﬁned as the maximum length of the
path connecting between nodes. For the DFG that can be
executed in the assumed CGRA, the depth is 32.
4.2
Adapting Kernel Processing and Control Structures to
the Target CGRAs
The collision kernel process showed two problems for exe-
cution at the CGRAs: indirect references and an imperfectly
nested loop.
An indirect reference requires multiple array accesses,
such as a[b[i]].
In cases of indirect reference, values
obtained from multiple memory accesses are fed into the
CGRA at runtime. This can create a bottleneck in memory
accesses, leading to insuﬃcient performance. However, if
the value of b[i] is known in advance due to the character-
istics of the application, it becomes just an array access. The
collision kernel is just such a case.
If the target process for the CGRAs is a perfectly nested
loop, the processing within the innermost loop can be directly
executed on the CGRAs. However, executing the process-
ing among the innermost loops becomes a challenge for an
imperfectly nested loop. For example, processing that over-
writes a variable will produce diﬀerent results if the number
of executions changes. Therefore, if variable renaming al-
lows the code to produce the same output for the same input
regardless of the number of executions, all processing can
be moved to the innermost loop. It transforms the loop into
a perfectly nested structure. Note that this transformation is
not applicable if the inter-loop processing involves reduction
operations.
The kernel targeted in this paper uses a uniﬁed ﬂoating-
point data type, allowing for switching between FP64 and
FP32. It is assumed that the CGRAs can perform operations
in FP32. As for the operation contents, no mathematical
functions were used, but the reduction operation for addition
was included. The other operations are shown in Table 1. In
the CGRAs assumed in this study, the reduction operation
can be performed in the PEs at the bottom row of the CGRA.

Although indirect references are included in the code, they
can be simply replaced with array accesses because the pat-
terns to be accessed are ﬁxed. As shown in Fig. 5, the code
comprises imperfectly nested loops; however, because inter-
loop processing does not involve reduction operations, it can
be incorporated into the innermost loop by renaming vari-
ables. Therefore, execution in CGRA is feasible.
4.3
Applying Loop Unrolling
Because the innermost loop is repeated 37 times in the LBM
target code, the loops can be unrolled by a factor of up
to 37.
The resources of the CGRA are 32 × 32 = 1024
for the number of operations, 32 × 2 = 64 for the number
of input data, and 32 for the number of output data. The
most restrictive constraint is the number of input data. For
example, as shown in Table 1, Loop 3 requires 41 input data.
However, when loop unrolling by a factor of 3 is applied, the
total number of input data increases to 25 + (15 + 1) × 3 =
73, which exceeds the limit of 64. Therefore, the process
unrolled by a factor of 3 for the Loop 3 cannot be executed
on the assumed CGRA. Thus, the maximum factor of loop
unrollings for Loops 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 that can be executed
within the single CGRA is 31, 4, 2, 4, and 3, respectively.
We try to consider a conﬁguration that applies loop
unrolling by a maximum factor to each innermost loop and
achieves maximum throughput. Because the innermost loop
requires 37 iterations, while loop 1 can be unrolled by a factor
of 31, Loop 1 requires two CGRAs to achieve maximum
throughput. Similarly, Loops 2, 3, 4, and 5 require 10, 19, 10,
and 13 CGRAs, respectively. Simply adding these together
would require 54 CGRAs.
When considering loop unrolling, it is important to note
that the number of input data includes constant values that do
not change during execution, even if they are array constants.
If the constant values can be kept inside the PE (as described
in Sect. 2.2), there is no need to input data to the CGRA
each cycle. It is necessary to fully unroll (by a factor of
37) the innermost to make the array constants inside the
PE. If Loop 3 is fully unrolled, the number of input data is
25+1×37 = 62, which is less than 64. In practice, however,
the single CGRA cannot execute it because the number of
operations does not meet the constraint. Similarly, the single
CGRA cannot execute a fully unrolled Loop 5 due to the
limited number of output data.
Full loop unrolling oﬀers additional advantages. Since
it eliminates the loop structure, the reduction operation can
be replaced by a summation of all elements.
This re-
placement eliminates the constraint imposed on the CGRAs,
which limited reduction operations to the bottom row. Also,
the overhead of recalculation caused by rewriting the pro-
cessing between loops, which existed in the imperfectly
nested loop structure, is eliminated.
In summary, loop unrolling by a factor of less than 37,
which is not fully unrolling, is a lot of the CGRAs to use due
to the limited number of input data. Therefore, we further
investigated the case of full loop unrolling.
4.4
Manually DFG Partitioning
The processing applied fully unrolled from Loop 1 to Loop 5
can be expressed as a single DFG. By partitioning this DFG
according to the constraints of the assumed CGRA, the num-
ber of CGRAs required can be determined. Assuming that
data transfer time is overlapped with operation time, exe-
cution performance can be estimated because the assumed
CGRAs give the calculation results in a ﬁxed number of
cycles (32).
Although full loop unrolling results in a single DFG, it
is necessary to consider where to partition the DFG based on
the loop structure in order to reduce the number of data inputs
and outputs. In particular, because the reduction operation
combines a large number of data into one, Loop 1, Loop 2,
and Loop 4, which include the reduction operations, should
be partitioned after the reduction operation in order to reduce
the amount of data transferred to the next process. Consid-
ering the number of operations in each loop, no combination
can be merged. Loop 3 requires partitioning into three due
to the limitation of the number of operations, while Loop 5
requires partitioning into two because the number of output
data is 37, exceeding the 32 that can be output by the single
CGRA. In addition, the processing between loops can be
combined with the loops before and after, and the policy was
to combine them with the DFG of the previous loop. As a
result of these considerations, the DFG partitioning is shown
in Table 2.
Since the assumed CGRAs support fma, part of fmul
and fadd are converted to fma. Additionally, the division
calculation cannot be performed directly, so it is converted
to two operations: frecpe and fmul. PE utilization is the
total number of operations required divided by 1024, which
is the number of PEs the CGRA has. The results show that
8 CGRAs are needed to compute the collision kernel.
4.5
DFG Partitioning using Integer Linear Programming
The larger the DFG, the more diﬃcult it is to partition the
DFG under the CGRA constraints. Therefore, it is important
to automate DFG partitioning.
The partitioning problem
is formulated as Integer Linear Programming (ILP) based
on [24]. Formulation and the results of DFG partitioning
using ILP are presented.
4.5.1
Formulation
The objective function of DFG partitioning is to minimize
the number of edges between the partitioned DFGs, equiva-
lent to minimizing the number of communications between
CGRAs. Inputs and variables required for this formulation
are described, and their constraints are given.

Experiments
The proposed formulation’s correctness is validated by ap-
plying it to the processing of Loop 5 (from the collision
kernel, without loop unrolling) and solving the resulting
problem using the ILP tool SCIP [25].
A DFG with 57
nodes and 56 edges is generated from Loop 5. Since load
and store operations are not assigned to PEs, removing them
results in a DFG with 22 nodes and 21 edges. Figure 6 shows
the result of partitioning this DFG into 3 DFGs to ﬁt a 4 × 4
CGRA (i.e., 16 nodes and depth 4). It requires only 2 DFGs
in terms of the number of nodes. However, it is partitioned
into 3 DFGs because the depth of the DFGs is greater than
4.

4.6
Performance Estimation
Since the assumed CGRA in this study has not yet undergone
detailed design or hardware implementation, actual evalua-
tion results from RTL simulation or a physical device are
not available. In this section, the execution performance of
LBM using the multiple CGRAs is estimated.
The execution time for a lattice size of 1024 × 8192 is
estimated for the CGRAs. Since 8 CGRAs are used, the
latency for one lattice operation is 32 × 8 = 256 cycles. If
the bandwidth between CGRA and memory is suﬃcient and
the data transfer and CGRA calculation can be overlapped,
data can be input every cycle, so the calculation of a lattice
of 1024 × 8192 requires 256 + 1024 × 8192 −1 = 8,388,863
cycles. Assuming operation at 1 GHz, this is approximately
8.39ms.

5.
Related Work
RIKEN CGRA has been proposed as a CGRA required in
the HPC ﬁeld [1]. RIKEN CGRA was designed to satisfy
the following three design concepts: 1) Be a modular design
for design space exploration, 2) Capability of ﬂoating-point
operations for HPC, 3) Stream computing model without
memory load/store inside the PE array. The RIKEN CGRA
is based on an elastic CGRA, and the connections between
PEs are diﬀerent from those of our assumed CGRA. The
computation results are not produced in ﬁxed cycles, which
means that the DFG partitioning method using ILP proposed
in this paper cannot be applied without modiﬁcations. How-
ever, because the RIKEN CGRA has a constant number of
registers, the loop unrolling approach discussed in this paper
is also applicable to the RIKEN CGRA.
While numerous papers address the co-design of
CGRAs and applications [2, 28, 29], these primarily focus
on architectural exploration. No publications to date have
investigated the focus on optimizing HPC applications from
a software perspective. In particular, the loop unrolling con-
siderations discussed in this paper are crucial for CGRA op-
timization because the loop unrolling determines the degree
of parallelism and, thus, the execution performance.
DFG partitioning is necessary to run huge DFGs in
CGRAs. Several methods to minimize the amount of data
transfer between CGRAs are proposed [24, 30].
Further-
more, as DFGs become larger, the number of possible par-
titioning combinations increases, making it diﬃcult to ﬁnd
a solution within a realistic timeframe.
To address this,
techniques and tools have been proposed that perform hier-
archical partitioning after abstracting the DFG. Speciﬁcally,
a tool called METIS [26, 27] is widely used, and there are
proposals to accelerate it by multithreading METIS [31] or
implementing it for GPUs [32], as well as proposals [33]
that leverage METIS as a base and incorporate critical path
considerations for partitioning, which are expected to im-
prove execution performance. To the best of our knowledge,
there is no DFG partitioning method with DFG depth as a
constraint.
Regarding CGRA compilation, numerous techniques
have been researched to accelerate mapping time.
For
mapping as well, techniques and tools that perform hi-
erarchical mapping after abstracting the DFG, such as
PANORAMA [17] and HierCGRA [18], have been pro-
posed. Other approaches include acceleration using cluster-
ing algorithms [19], techniques that separate mapping into
time and space [20], and methods using reinforcement learn-
ing [21]. PANORAMA [17] was published in 2022, while
the others were published in 2024 or 2025, suggesting that
many researchers are working on accelerating mapping.
As for studies on LBM acceleration, there are case stud-
ies of GPU acceleration [8] and FPGA acceleration [34]. For
GPU, it achieved 1,544 GFlops for the collision kernel of the
D2Q37 LBM on a K80 GPU with TDP 300W. In FPGA,
519.3 GFlops was achieved with the D2Q9 model. There is
another study that estimated the LBM of the D3Q27 model
when implemented in an ASIC [35]. No publications were
found implementing the D2Q37 LBM on CGRAs.
6.
Conclusions
This paper investigates techniques for executing large HPC
applications on CGRAs. The optimization of LBM, a large-
scale application in the HPC ﬁeld, is examined as a case
study. Analysis of loop unrolling showed that full loop un-
rolling signiﬁcantly improves performance by reducing the
amount of input data required by the CGRA. Furthermore,
this paper proposes the DFG partitioning method based on
an ILP formulation constrained by DFG depth. The high
performance achieved in this case study suggests the eﬀec-
tiveness of these techniques for broader application in HPC.
